title: Water, the Uncarved Block and Simplicity
bigQuestion: Why do the Daodejing and the Zhuangzi teach with pictures instead of rules?

story.title: The Knife That Stayed Sharp
story.kicker: A cook's knife stays sharp for nineteen years, and a king asks him how.
paragraphs: In a story from the Zhuangzi, a king named Wenhui watched his cook, Ding, cut up an ox. Ding's hands moved and his shoulders turned. His knife made a soft, even sound, like music. The work looked like a dance.
'Amazing!' said the king. 'How did your skill get this good?' Cook Ding put down his knife. 'What I care about is the Way,' he said. 'It goes beyond skill.'

Ding explained. When he began, he saw only a whole ox in front of him. After three years, he no longer saw the whole ox. Now he felt his way through it. He let his knife follow the natural gaps between the joints.

'A good cook changes his knife every year, because he cuts,' Ding said. 'An ordinary cook changes it every month, because he hacks. I have had this knife for nineteen years. It is still as sharp as the day it was made.'
The king was quiet for a moment. Then he said, 'Wonderful! From the words of Cook Ding, I have learned how to care for life.' People have retold this story for more than 2,000 years.
story.think: What do you think the king learned about life from a cook's knife?

lessons.title: The Highest Good Is Like Water
lessons.mainIdea: Daodejing 8 says the highest good is like water, which helps all things, does not compete and goes to low places.
reading: Water is one of the Daodejing's favorite *images*. An image is a picture in words. Chapter 8 says the highest good is like water. It returns to water again and again.
Why water? The chapter says water benefits all things. It does not fight or compete. It settles in low places that people avoid. The chapter says this makes water close to the Dao.
Readers see a lesson about humility here. Water does not rush to the top. It goes low, and yet everything needs it. Many readers see this as a picture of helping without showing off.

words.d: a picture in words that helps explain an idea
not thinking you are more important than others

lessons.title: Soft Overcomes Hard
lessons.mainIdea: The Daodejing says the soft and weak overcome the hard and strong, as water wears away stone.
reading: Chapter 78 says nothing in the world is softer or weaker than water. Yet for attacking what is hard and strong, nothing can beat it. It is a surprising claim about something so gentle.

Chapter 76 adds another picture. When people are alive, their bodies are soft and bendable. When they die, they become stiff. Green plants are soft and supple; dry ones snap. So the book links softness with life.
Readers use these chapters in many ways. Some see advice about patience. Some see a lesson about gentleness in conflict. Martial arts teachers have often quoted the idea too.

words.d: able to bend easily without breaking
to win against or get past something difficult

look.title: Daodejing 78

check.why: Living things are soft and supple; dead things are stiff.

check.q: What does supple mean?
check.why: Supple means able to bend easily.

lessons.title: The Empty Hub
lessons.mainIdea: Daodejing 11 says the empty space in a wheel's hub, a bowl and a room is what makes them useful.
reading: Chapter 11 gives three pictures. Thirty spokes meet at a wheel's hub. It is the empty space at the center, where the axle goes, that makes the wheel useful.
Next, clay is shaped into a bowl. It is the empty space inside that holds food. Then doors and windows are cut into a room. It is the empty space that makes the room usable.
The chapter ends by saying that what is there gives benefit, but what is not there gives use. Readers see a lesson: emptiness and quiet can matter as much as things.

words.d: the center of a wheel, where the spokes meet
open, empty space; in the Daodejing, what makes things useful

lessons.title: The Uncarved Block
lessons.mainIdea: The Daodejing uses pu, the uncarved block of wood, as a picture of simplicity before things are shaped or divided.
reading: Another image is *pu*, the uncarved block. Pu is a piece of wood that has not yet been carved into anything. It is plain, whole and full of possibility.
Chapter 19 advises showing plainness and holding on to the uncarved block. Chapter 28 speaks of returning to the uncarved block. The book links it to having fewer wants.
Readers interpret pu in different ways. Some see it as the simple heart a person has before learning to show off. Others see a picture of the Dao itself, before it is divided into many things.

words.d: the uncarved block; plain, whole simplicity in the Daodejing

look.title: Before the Carving
look.text: A woodcarver holds a plain block of wood. It could become a spoon, a bowl, a bird or a box. Once it is carved into a spoon, it can no longer become a bowl. The Daodejing praises the block before carving.
look.prompt: Why might the Daodejing praise the block more than the finished spoon?

check.q: What is pu?
check.why: Pu is the uncarved block of wood.

check.q: What does the uncarved block stand for, in the Daodejing?
check.why: It is a picture of plain, whole simplicity.

check.q: Which chapter speaks of returning to the uncarved block?
check.why: Chapter 28 speaks of returning to pu.

lessons.title: The Small Village
lessons.mainIdea: Daodejing 80 pictures a small, peaceful village whose people are content with a simple life.
reading: Chapter 80 describes a small state with few people. They have tools and boats but seldom use them. They enjoy their food, their clothes and their homes.
The neighboring village is so close that people can hear its roosters and dogs. Yet, the chapter says, people grow old and die without ever visiting it. They are content where they are.
Readers argue about this chapter. Some read it as a picture of peace and contentment. Others see it as an ideal that could never fully work. Some compare it to modern calls to slow down.

words.d: a picture of how things would be at their best

look.title: A Picture of Chapter 80
look.text: A few houses sit by a river. Smoke rises from cooking fires. Across the field, a rooster crows in the next village. A grandmother hears it, smiles and goes back to her garden. She has never needed to go there.
look.prompt: Would you want to live in this village? What would be good about it, and what would be hard?

check.q: What can people hear from the next village in chapter 80?
check.why: Chapter 80 says they can hear its roosters and dogs.

check.q: What does content mean?
check.why: Content means satisfied with what you have.

check.q: How do readers respond to chapter 80?
choices: All agree it is a map
Some see peace; others see an ideal that could not fully work
check.why: Readers disagree about how to read it.

lessons.title: Knowing When You Have Enough
lessons.mainIdea: The Daodejing teaches that knowing when you have enough brings contentment.
reading: Several chapters talk about wanting less. Chapter 46 says there is no greater trouble than not knowing when you have enough. It says the person who knows enough is always content.
Chapter 44 asks hard questions. Which matters more, your name or your life? Your life or your things? It says knowing when to stop keeps a person from danger.
Many Daoist readers link this to simplicity and the uncarved block. Other traditions have similar teachings. Readers compare them while noticing each tradition's own reasons.

words.d: a calm feeling of being satisfied

look.title: Daodejing 46

check.q: Which image do Daoist readers link to wanting less?
check.why: They link wanting less to simplicity and pu.

lessons.title: Cook Ding's Knife
lessons.mainIdea: In Zhuangzi 3, Cook Ding's knife stays sharp for 19 years because he follows the natural gaps.
reading: The story of Cook Ding is in chapter 3 of the Zhuangzi. The chapter is often titled 'The Secret of Caring for Life.' Ding cuts an ox so smoothly that it looks like a dance.
Ding says he follows the natural lines and gaps. He does not hack at bone. So his knife stays sharp for 19 years, while other cooks must replace theirs often.
Readers link this story to wu wei. Ding acts with great skill but without forcing. When he reaches a hard spot, he slows down and takes care. The king says he has learned how to care for life.

words.d: the cook in Zhuangzi 3 whose knife stayed sharp by following natural gaps
the ability to do something well, from practice

lessons.title: The Frog in the Well
lessons.mainIdea: In Zhuangzi 17, a frog in a well thinks its small world is everything until a great turtle describes the sea.
reading: Chapter 17 of the Zhuangzi, 'Autumn Floods,' tells of a frog living in a broken-down well. The frog loves its well. It splashes in the water and rests on the edge.
The frog invites a great turtle from the Eastern Sea to come in. But the turtle cannot even fit its leg in. The turtle describes the sea: so huge that floods and droughts barely change it.

The frog is stunned. Readers use this story to talk about limited views. From the bottom of a well, the sky looks small. Today, 'a frog in a well' is a common Chinese saying for someone with a narrow view.

words.d: the way something looks from where you stand

look.title: The View from the Well
look.text: The frog looks up from the bottom of the well. It sees a small, round patch of sky. 'That is the whole sky,' it says. The turtle, who has swum the open sea, knows the sky stretches to every horizon.
look.prompt: When have you learned that your view of something was too small?

check.q: Which chapter of the Zhuangzi has the frog in the well?
check.why: It is in chapter 17, 'Autumn Floods.'

check.q: Who describes the sea to the frog?
check.why: A turtle from the Eastern Sea describes it.

check.q: What does 'a frog in a well' mean as a saying?
check.why: It names someone whose view is limited.

lessons.title: Why Teach With Pictures?
lessons.mainIdea: The Daodejing and the Zhuangzi teach with images and stories, which readers can interpret in many ways.
reading: The Analects often gives direct advice about how to act. The Daodejing and Zhuangzi more often give images: water, a hub, a block of wood, a cook, a frog.

An image does not tell you exactly what to think. It asks you to look and wonder. That is one reason these books have so many interpretations. Different readers notice different things in the same picture.
Zhuangzi's stories are also often funny. Scholars note that humor can help people let go of fixed ideas. The images stay in readers' minds long after they finish reading.
